title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 21: David v. Arroyo: Constitutionality of Proclaiming a State of National Emergency

primary_topics: Chapter 21 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of David v. Arroyo, in which the Court, through Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez, sustained Presidential Proclamation 1017 only insofar as it called out the Armed Forces to prevent or suppress lawless violence, while striking down its extraneous provisions and the 'acts of terrorism' portion of General Order No. 5.

The three-part dissection of PP 1017's operative portion: the calling-out power under Section 18 of Article VII, the faithful-execution clause that could not be stretched into a power to issue decrees, and the declaration of a state of national emergency under Section 17 of Article XII, which confers no power to take over private utilities without a delegation from Congress.

The catalogue of unconstitutional acts committed under the proclamation -- the warrantless arrests of Randolf David and Ronald Llamas, the dispersal of the KMU and NAFLU-KMU rallies on the wholesale cancellation of permits, the raid on the Daily Tribune and the warnings to media -- which the Court called plain censorship and a blatant disregard of constitutional rights.

CJP's own Concurring Opinion, reproduced in toto and treated by the ponente as an integral part of the ponencia, answering Justice Tinga's Dissent: PP 1017 might be a paper tiger, but it had nuclear teeth that had to be defanged, and the Court had to set the parameters of power lest those testing the outer limits of presidential prerogative one day burn down the country.

The separate opinions that frame the ruling: Justice Ynares-Santiago's concurrence insisting that the 'national emergency' of Article XII is economic rather than political, and Justice Tinga's dissent, joined by Justices Corona and Velasco, that the proclamation was an utter superfluity and the Decision an immodest show of brawn.
sub_topics: The Decision opened with a paean to liberty quoting the Chief Justice's philosophy that in cases involving liberty the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak.

The facts: on February 24, 2006, as the country marked the 20th Anniversary of EDSA People Power I, President Arroyo issued PP 1017 declaring a state of national emergency and GO 5 implementing it, lifting them a week later through PP 1021 after seven Petitions had been filed.
Respondents justified the issuances by a conspiracy to unseat or assassinate the President allegedly hatched by some military officers, leftist insurgents and members of the political opposition.

Malacanang cancelled all programs for the EDSA anniversary and revoked rally permits issued by local governments, and Presidential Chief of Staff Michael Defensor announced that warrantless arrests and the takeover of facilities, including media, could already be implemented.

KMU and NAFLU-KMU members marched toward the EDSA shrine anyway; protesters were violently dispersed, and UP professor and columnist Randolf S. David and Akbayan president Ronald Llamas were arrested without warrant.

On February 25, 2006 CIDG operatives raided the Daily Tribune offices and confiscated news stories, documents, pictures and mock-ups, with police stationed at the Tribune and at the pro-opposition papers Malaya and Abante.

Mootness: by 11-3-1 the Court held that PP 1021 did not moot the Petitions, since illegal acts had been committed during the eight days PP 1017 was operative and an unconstitutional act confers no rights and imposes no duties.

The four exceptions to mootness -- grave constitutional violation, exceptional character and paramount public interest, the need for controlling principles, and capability of repetition yet evading review -- were all present, reinforced by CJP's Separate Opinion in Sanlakas v. Executive Secretary.

Standing: David, Llamas, Cacho-Olivares and the Tribune Publishing Co. had alleged direct injury from illegal arrests and unlawful searches, and the other petitioners were heard on the ground of transcendental importance; impleading the sitting President as respondent was improper.

Review of factual bases: following Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Zamora and Lansang v. Garcia, the standard is arbitrariness rather than correctness, and the burden lies on the petitioner to show the President's decision totally bereft of factual basis -- a burden petitioners failed to carry against the solicitor general's detailed narration.

Facial challenge rejected: the overbreadth doctrine is a tool for testing statutes in free-speech cases, facial invalidation is a manifestly strong medicine to be used sparingly and only as a last resort, and a petitioner must establish that there can be no instance in which the assailed measure might be valid.
Vagueness rejected as well, since the doctrine requires a showing that the measure is vague in all its possible applications and petitioners made no such attempt.

First provision -- the calling-out power: per Sanlakas the Commander-in-Chief clause grants a sequence of graduated powers from the calling-out power through suspension of the writ to martial law, the sole criterion being necessity to prevent or suppress lawless violence, invasion or rebellion, with every act beyond it ultra vires.

The Court distinguished a declaration of a 'state of rebellion,' which merely announces a condition of public moment under the Administrative Code, from a proclamation of national emergency invoking Section 17 of Article XII -- an awesome power that could not be dismissed as harmless, as Sanlakas had done.

PP 1017 was emphatically not a declaration of martial law and could not justify warrantless arrests and seizures, a ban on public assemblies, press censorship or media takeover, or the issuance of presidential decrees.

Second provision -- faithful execution: the President's ordinance power is limited by the Administrative Code of 1987, legislative power belongs to Congress under the present Constitution, and the military may be ordered to enforce only laws pertinent to suppressing lawless violence, not civil or customs laws.

Third provision -- the state of national emergency: Section 17 of Article XII must be read with Section 23 of Article VI, so that the takeover of a private utility or business affected with public interest requires a delegation from Congress, the President being unable to decide alone whether the exceptional circumstances exist, when they cease, or which businesses to take over.
Void-as-applied: courts are not at liberty to invalidate a measure merely because it has been abused or misabused, and nothing in PP 1017 allowed the police to conduct illegal arrests or searches.

GO 5 and terrorism: 'lawless violence' is extant in the statutes and the Constitution, but Congress has yet to define and punish 'acts of terrorism,' so the President alone would decide what terrorism means -- a judgment absolute and without restriction, inviting indiscriminate arrests, raids, media takeovers and dispersals, and therefore unconstitutional as to that portion.

The arrest of David was unjustified: the officers could invoke only their observation of rallyists wearing 'Oust Gloria Now' shirts and their erroneous assumption that he led the rally, and the inquest prosecutor ordered his release after seven hours for insufficiency of evidence.

The dispersal and arrest of KMU members rested on Malacanang's arbitrary wholesale cancellation of permits, in disregard of the rule that freedom of assembly may be limited only upon a showing of clear and present danger, tolerance being the rule and limitation the exception, and of BP 880's requirement of notice and hearing before revocation.

The Tribune raid violated Rule 126 of the Rules of Court and the freedom of the press: the seizure of materials for publication, the stationing of policemen and the arrogant warnings to media were plain censorship, and the Court invoked the motto Obsta principiis.

The Court's reproduced summation held PP 1017 constitutional as a call to the AFP, its extraneous decree-issuing, law-enforcement-at-large and media-restraint provisions ultra vires, GO 5 valid except for 'acts of terrorism,' and the four enumerated acts unauthorized -- while refusing, on elementary due process, to impose sanctions on unidentified individual officers.

CJP's Concurring Opinion regretted that unanimity had been impossible after the EO 464 and CPR rulings, disagreed with the Dissent that the President could lawfully reissue PP 1017 as worded, and warned that those testing the outer limits of presidential prerogative were playing with fire.

Justice Ynares-Santiago concurred that the calling-out power authorizes neither decrees nor warrantless searches nor prior restraint, and argued that Section 17 of Article XII, sitting in the article on National Economy and Patrimony, presupposes an economic rather than a political emergency.

Justice Tinga, joined by Justices Corona and Velasco, dissented from Sanlakas, which he had written: PP 1017 was valid on its face, the comma in the phrase 'to all the laws and to all decrees' showed the President had not arrogated the power to issue decrees, terrorism is already encompassed by extant penal laws, and the majority had adjudicated David's injuries with undue haste, without trial and without impleading the officers -- leaving the ruling, in his closing words, to be read as an extended advisory opinion.

stances.claim: PP 1017 is constitutional only insofar as it calls upon the Armed Forces to prevent or suppress lawless violence; its extraneous provisions giving the President power to issue decrees, to direct the military to enforce all laws unrelated to lawless violence, and to impose standards on media or prior restraint on the press are ultra vires and unconstitutional.
stances.rhetorical_move: provision-by-provision severance: dividing the operative text into three clauses and matching each to the constitutional source that could or could not sustain it

stances.claim: Because Congress has never defined or made punishable 'acts of terrorism,' that portion of GO 5 must fall, for otherwise the President alone would determine what terrorism means, a judgment absolute and without restriction that would license indiscriminate arrests, raids on offices and residences, media takeovers and the dispersal of assemblies unfriendly to the administration.
stances.rhetorical_move: argument from the nullum crimen principle, followed by a concrete parade of the abuses an undefined standard would authorize

stances.claim: Under Section 17 of Article XII the President may declare a state of national emergency on her own, but in the absence of legislation she cannot take over a privately owned public utility or a private business affected with public interest, because emergency powers of that kind are reposed in Congress and must be delegated on reasonable terms.
stances.rhetorical_move: structural reading pairing Article XII, Section 17 with Article VI, Section 23 to separate the power to declare from the power to act

stances.claim: PP 1017 may be a paper tiger, but it has nuclear teeth that must indeed be defanged; some of its drafters were testing the outer limits of presidential prerogatives and the perseverance of the Court, and history would never forgive a Court that refused to strike down abuse at its inception.
stances.rhetorical_move: direct rebuttal of the Dissent's own metaphor, escalated through the images of nuclear teeth, playing with fire and historical judgment

stances.claim: Justice Tinga maintained that PP 1017 was valid on its face, an utter superfluity of no legal significance, and that in taking cognizance of the Petitions the Court had made an immodest show of brawn and placed itself in the business of defanging paper tigers, prejudging cases without a trial of facts or the impleading of the officers concerned.
stances.rhetorical_move: reported dissent, grounded in his own earlier ponencia in Sanlakas and in a close grammatical reading of the proclamation's comma and conjunctions

stances.claim: Justice Ynares-Santiago concurred but insisted that Section 17 of Article XII, situated in the article on National Economy and Patrimony, presupposes a national emergency that is economic and not political in nature, and that government action to stifle constitutional liberties cannot be preemptive against merely perceived or potential threats.
stances.rhetorical_move: reported concurrence arguing from the placement of the provision within the constitutional text

notable_anecdotes: The emergency was proclaimed on the very day the country celebrated the 20th Anniversary of EDSA People Power I, and the Office of the President promptly cancelled all the anniversary programs and revoked the rally permits local governments had already issued.
Presidential Chief of Staff Michael Defensor announced publicly that warrantless arrests and the takeover of facilities, including media, could already be implemented.

Before dawn on February 25, 2006 CIDG operatives raided the Daily Tribune, confiscating news stories, documents, pictures and the mock-ups of the Saturday issue, and posted policemen at Malaya and Abante as well.

Randolf David was arrested because officers saw rallyists in 'Oust Gloria Now' t-shirts and assumed he was the leader; he was not even wearing the shirt, and the inquest prosecutor ordered his release after seven hours for insufficiency of evidence.

CJP records that he hoped until the last moment of deliberations for a unanimous Court, since in the preceding two weeks it had decided the EO 464 and Calibrated Preemptive Response cases with one voice, and that Justice Tinga's Dissent made that hope an impossibility.
Answering the Dissent's 'paper tiger,' CJP borrowed the colorful words of an erstwhile Asian leader to say the proclamation had nuclear teeth that must indeed be defanged.

He closed his concurrence with a historical reproach: the country might never have experienced the wrenching pain of dictatorship, and a past President might not have fallen into the precipice of authoritarianism, had the Supreme Court then had the moral courage to remind him of his mortality.
Justice Tinga ended his Dissent by predicting that when the passions of the times died down and sober retrospect acceded, the Decision would be looked upon as an extended advisory opinion.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 21 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests David v. Arroyo, the challenge to Presidential Proclamation 1017 and General Order No. 5, issued on February 24, 2006 as the country marked the 20th anniversary of EDSA People Power I and lifted eight days later by PP 1021. In that interval the EDSA celebrations were cancelled, rally permits were revoked wholesale, KMU and NAFLU-KMU marchers were violently dispersed, Randolf David and Ronald Llamas were arrested without warrant, and CIDG operatives raided the Daily Tribune. Writing for the Court, Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez held the Petitions not moot, since an unconstitutional act confers no rights and the case was capable of repetition yet evading review; upheld standing on direct injury and transcendental importance; and, applying the arbitrariness standard of Lansang and Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Zamora, found the President justified in calling out the Armed Forces because petitioners had not shown the proclamation factually baseless. Facial challenges for overbreadth and vagueness failed, facial invalidation being a manifestly strong medicine. Dividing the operative text in three, the Court sustained the calling-out clause under Section 18 of Article VII, denied that the faithful-execution clause let the President issue decrees or direct the military to enforce unrelated laws, and held that a declared national emergency under Section 17 of Article XII confers no power to take over private utilities without a congressional delegation under Section 23 of Article VI. GO 5 was valid except for 'acts of terrorism,' undefined by Congress and therefore left to the President's absolute judgment. The warrantless arrests, the permit cancellations made without notice or hearing, and the Tribune raid and warnings to media were declared unauthorized and plain censorship, though due process barred sanctioning unnamed officers. The chapter reproduces in full CJP's Concurring Opinion, which the ponente treated as integral: regretting the loss of unanimity, he answered Justice Tinga's Dissent that PP 1017 might be a paper tiger but had nuclear teeth that must be defanged, warned that its drafters were testing the outer limits of presidential prerogatives and playing with fire, and recalled that an earlier Court's want of moral courage had let a past President fall into the precipice of authoritarianism. Justice Ynares-Santiago's concurrence and Justice Tinga's dissent, joined by Justices Corona and Velasco, close the chapter.
